new_statements.quote: Tone and stress are combined in a complex unit which usually occurs in connection with the grammatical stem. Angaataha, with four tonemes, is noticeably different from the other Angan languages. In Angaataha stress is also linked to high tone. Thus Angaataha is like a 'tone language' and the others are more 'intonation languages'. [p. 87] || No phonemic analysis of Simbari was available. So the comments here are necessarily tentative. [...] At this stage other features are assumed to be the same as Baruya. [p. 63]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level only: across the twelve Angan languages Lloyd surveyed (Simbari included), pitch and stress form a single prominence unit that is usually located on the grammatical stem of the word; Angaataha is the one tonal (4-toneme) member, the rest, Simbari among them, are 'intonation languages'. For Simbari itself Lloyd had only a survey wordlist (collected by D. Best), explicitly states that no phonemic analysis existed, and assumes its unlisted features match Baruya; nothing is said about where Simbari word stress falls.
new_statements.exceptions: Angaataha (tonal, stress linked to high tone) is singled out as different from the rest of the family.
new_statements.domain_note: Generalisation over the Angan family, not a Simbari description; prominence located relative to the stem (word/morphological domain). Vowel length is said to be slightly greater in stressed syllables and in short words (p. 87).
new_statements.identity_note: Simbari = Chimbari (Glottolog simb1255, ISO smb); the same people are Herdt's 'Sambia'. Lloyd 1973 places them in the lower Yaiga Valley with a Baruya-Simbari subgroup; Wikipedia notes at least two dialects, none described. The only stress remark found is a generalisation over the whole Angan family, not a statement about Simbari or any Simbari dialect.
